name: Work Items List
one_liner: The prioritised list of everything to be built: stories, enablers, bugs.
purpose: As part of the Development Work Plan, the Work Items List (WIL) is the list of the work to be done during a project — typically defects, enabler stories and user stories — intended to be prioritised, effort-estimated and tracked in terms of progress. The Product Owner maintains it continuously throughout the entire project, revisiting it each iteration with the Business Manager and the Business Implementation Group and then discussing it with the A-PCT so relative estimates and dependencies can be set. A work item is not a contract between the team and the Product Owner but a pointer to something that needs to be implemented.

fields.what: A story written in user-focused language: a small vertical slice of system behaviour, implemented by the A-PCT inside one iteration.
fields.pollux: 'As a Board Secretariat user I see total exposure by member state on one page' — 8 points.

fields.what: A story with an enablement perspective: architecture, infrastructure, evaluating options, legal compliance, continuous improvement and other non-functional work.
fields.pollux: WIL-003: read-only replica of the CASTOR lending platform with a nightly delta load — 20 points.

fields.what: Bugs are work items too: they sit in the same list, prioritised and estimated alongside stories.
fields.pollux: BUG-112: maturity bucket boundary rounds one day earlier than the accounts — 3 points.

fields.what: Every item is prioritised. Prioritisation, not completeness, is what lets the team start work.
fields.pollux: MoSCoW plus release tag; Curie re-ranks the top twenty items at every Release Planning.

fields.what: Items are effort-estimated — relative estimates in points, given by the team, not by the Product Owner.
fields.pollux: Planning poker in the refinement session; Lamarr's 20-point replica estimate survived challenge.

fields.what: Work items are tracked in terms of progress — they are the unit progress is measured in.
fields.pollux: Delivered points per iteration feed both burndown charts and the Development Status Report.

fields.what: A work item is not a contract between the team and the PrOw but a pointer to something that needs implementing.
fields.pollux: Each POLLUX story links to the reconciliation rules and the UI sketch rather than restating them.

fields.what: Each item commonly refers to additional relevant information — business rules, diagrams, user interface specifications.
fields.pollux: Reconciliation stories point to Finance's rule set; access stories point to the DPC's assessment.

fields.what: The Features list defined in the Project Charter is the key generator of the work items that populate the WIL.
fields.pollux: Charter features F1–F4 decomposed into 61 user stories before the RfE gate.

fields.what: The Architecture Overview and Operational Model are an important source of the enabler stories supporting the business part.
fields.pollux: Einstein's four building blocks produced 24 enabler stories, three of them Must for Release 1.

fields.what: Release Planning, Iteration Review and Iteration Retrospective continuously provide inputs and generate new work items.
fields.pollux: The review that exposed the missing data-protection check generated two new enabler stories.

fields.what: Change requests, risks, issues and decisions generate work items: a change request becomes stories, a risk mitigation becomes enablers.
fields.pollux: Risk R3 (single-point data-engineering knowledge) generated a pairing enabler in iteration 5.

fields.what: Maintaining the WIL updated and prioritised is the Product Owner's responsibility, ensuring the team always works on the most relevant items.
fields.pollux: Curie owns it outright; nobody argues with her acceptance criteria.

fields.what: As the Project Owner's representative in daily project life, the BM supports the PrOw with business priorities, objectives and user needs.
fields.who: BM Supports — unusually, S not I
fields.pollux: Hopper's Release 2 argument with Curie is settled by the guide: the PrOw decides the list.

fields.what: Consulted by team and PrOw to guarantee the list's consistency and form, and by the PM to verify alignment with the Charter.
fields.who: TeCo Consulted — the only agile C for TeCo
fields.pollux: Lovelace enforces the story template so items are workable, not prettier.

fields.what: Each iteration the PrOw, the Business Implementation Group and the BM revisit the list to keep it relevant.
fields.pollux: Curie, Hopper and the Risk/Finance user representatives meet mid-iteration to refresh the top of the list.

fields.what: The WIL need not be complete for the A-PCT to start, but it must be prioritised or resources go to unimportant items.
fields.pollux: Only Release 1 was detailed at the RfE gate; Release 4 was four unestimated headings.

fields.f: Balance of business and enabler work
fields.what: Only business items and the architecture collapses; only enablers and users get nothing — the ArOw helps find the balance.
fields.pollux: Einstein wanted three enabler iterations first; the agreed rule is enablers ride in every release.

fields.what: BM S · PM A · TeCo C · PrOw R · ArOw S · ATeM S — the only agile row with BM = S and TeCo = C.
fields.pollux: Curie responsible, Hopper supporting, Lovelace consulted, you accountable for charter alignment.
